item.title: Maynilad has undertaken nearly ₱10 billion in La Mesa upgrades to strengthen water supply resilience
item.dc:creator: Danica Pagarigan
item.description: West Zone concessionaire Maynilad Water Services, Inc. (Maynilad) has undertaken nearly ₱10 billion worth of rehabilitation and improvement works at its La Mesa facilities over several years, covering completed and ongoing projects that strengthen its ability to manage changing raw water conditions as it prepares for potentially drier conditions ahead. The major rehabilitation and improvement […]
item.content:encoded:
West Zone concessionaire Maynilad Water Services, Inc. (Maynilad) has undertaken nearly ₱10 billion worth of rehabilitation and improvement works at its La Mesa facilities over several years, covering completed and ongoing projects that strengthen its ability to manage changing raw water conditions as it prepares for potentially drier conditions ahead.

The major rehabilitation and improvement works cover treatment improvements, enhanced water recovery and raw water augmentation systems, additional raw water storage, and related facility upgrades. The nearly ₱10-billion amount covers completed and ongoing works.

Among the key improvements is the upgrading of La Mesa Water Treatment Plant 1 (LMTP1) from an original raw water turbidity design capability of around 300 nephelometric turbidity units (NTU) to a peak design capability of 2,000 NTU. Similar improvement works are ongoing at LMTP2 to raise its treatment capability to the same level.

The enhancements significantly expand the range of raw water conditions that the facilities can manage. The Angat-Ipo system has experienced episodes of substantially higher turbidity over the years, including levels reaching around 1,800 NTU in 2012.

Maynilad has also enhanced its water recovery and raw water augmentation systems. Once all three systems are fully operational, they are designed to provide a combined recovery and augmentation capacity of approximately 125–170 million liters per day (MLD). Recovery Systems 1 and 3 are already operational, while Recovery System 2 is targeted for completion in December 2026.

Another key component is the conversion of former sludge lagoons into dedicated raw water reservoirs. Lagoons 3 and 4 currently provide approximately 133 million liters of storage, equivalent to about two-thirds of the planned 200-million-liter total capacity.

The reservoirs provide an additional operating buffer during periods of reduced Angat-Ipo inflow or adjustments in raw water allocation, giving Maynilad greater flexibility in managing available raw water during dry periods.

The La Mesa treatment plants have a combined design capacity of 2,400 MLD. LMTP1 has a design capacity of 1,500 MLD, while LMTP2 has a design capacity of 900 MLD.

Maynilad’s continuing rehabilitation and process improvements at La Mesa include enhancements to sedimentation, filtration, sludge management, monitoring and control systems, as well as the replacement of aging equipment and other facility improvements.

“We continue to invest in La Mesa because water supply resilience depends not only on how much raw water is available, but also on how efficiently we can treat, recover and manage the water already within our system,” said Maynilad Chief Operating Officer Christopher Jaime T. Lichauco.

“These improvements give us additional operating flexibility as raw water conditions change and support our continuing preparations for potentially drier conditions associated with El Niño,” he added.

The La Mesa improvements support Maynilad’s broader water supply resilience strategy, alongside the development of alternative sources, continued reduction of non-revenue water, additional storage, and improvements to its distribution network.

PHOTO CAPTION: WATER SUPPLY RESILIENCE. Maynilad’s La Mesa water treatment facilities and the ongoing conversion of former sludge lagoons into raw water reservoirs. Nearly ₱10 billion worth of major rehabilitation and improvement works are being undertaken at La Mesa to strengthen treatment capability, enhance water recovery and raw water augmentation, expand storage, and provide greater operational flexibility under changing raw water conditions.

item.title: Maynilad completes ₱200-M pipe upgrade project in Las Piñas City
item.dc:creator: Danica Pagarigan
item.description: West Zone concessionaire Maynilad Water Services, Inc. (Maynilad) completed a ₱200-million pipe replacement project in Las Piñas City, upgrading more than 23 kilometers of aging pipelines to improve water pressure for around 50,000 customers. The project involved the replacement of 23.11 kilometers of old, leaky, and undersized pipes ranging from 75mm to 300mm in diameter. […]
item.content:encoded:
West Zone concessionaire Maynilad Water Services, Inc. (Maynilad) completed a ₱200-million pipe replacement project in Las Piñas City, upgrading more than 23 kilometers of aging pipelines to improve water pressure for around 50,000 customers.

The project involved the replacement of 23.11 kilometers of old, leaky, and undersized pipes ranging from 75mm to 300mm in diameter. These upgrades enabled the recovery of about 3.73 million liters per day (MLD) of water, supporting Maynilad’s ongoing efforts to reduce system water losses and improve overall network efficiency.

The upgrades have improved water pressure in the project areas, with pressure levels increasing from around 4 pounds per square inch (psi) to 16 psi. At this pressure, water can reach up to the third storey of a structure without the need for a booster pump, depending on the building’s elevation and internal plumbing conditions.

The project benefits customers in barangays Manuyo Dos, Talon Singko, Talon Uno, Talon Tres, and Pulang Lupa Dos.

Completed in 2025, the Las Piñas pipe replacement project forms part of Maynilad’s Non-Revenue Water (NRW) Management Program, which focuses on reducing water losses and improving system efficiency through the establishment of District Metered Areas (DMAs), advanced network diagnostics, active leak detection and repair, pipe replacement initiatives, and strict meter management.

“By replacing aging, leaky, and undersized pipelines, we are strengthening our distribution network to better accommodate growing demand while ensuring the continued delivery of safe, reliable, and sustainable water services,” said Maynilad President and CEO Ramoncito S. Fernandez. “These investments are essential to improving system efficiency and reducing water losses across our service area.”

Maynilad operates the largest water concession by population served within a single concession area in the Philippines. It is a concessionaire of the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS) for the West Zone of the Greater Manila Area, which is composed of the cities of Manila (certain portions), Quezon City (certain portions), Makati (west of South Super Highway), Caloocan, Pasay, Parañaque, Las Piñas, Muntinlupa, Valenzuela, Navotas and Malabon, all in Metro Manila; the cities of Cavite, Bacoor and Imus, and the municipalities of Kawit, Noveleta and Rosario, all in Cavite Province.

item.title: El Niño and Water Supply: What Maynilad Customers Should Know
item.dc:creator: author@example.invalid
item.description: Maynilad continues to strengthen water supply reliability through long-term investments in alternative and supplemental sources, water treatment and storage, water loss reduction, and distribution network improvements. These measures also help the company manage changing weather and raw water conditions, including those associated with El Niño. Below are answers to common questions about El Niño, Maynilad’s […]
item.content:encoded:
Maynilad continues to strengthen water supply reliability through long-term investments in alternative and supplemental sources, water treatment and storage, water loss reduction, and distribution network improvements. These measures also help the company manage changing weather and raw water conditions, including those associated with El Niño.

Below are answers to common questions about El Niño, Maynilad’s preparedness, and responsible water use.

1. What is El Niño, and how can it affect water supply?

El Niño is a climate phenomenon associated with unusually warm sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. It can influence weather patterns and, in the Philippines, may contribute to below-normal rainfall in some areas. Less rainfall over time can reduce the replenishment of dams and other water sources. The extent of any effect on water service depends on actual weather, available raw water, treatment and distribution conditions, and measures taken to manage supply.

2. Does El Niño automatically mean there will be water interruptions?

No. El Niño does not automatically result in service interruptions. Maynilad manages available water through a combination of supply sources, treatment facilities, storage, water loss reduction, and distribution network operations. Service conditions depend on several factors, including raw water availability and quality, production capacity, and network conditions. If a supply-related adjustment affecting customers becomes necessary, Maynilad will issue appropriate area-specific advisories.

3. How is Maynilad preparing for El Niño?

Maynilad’s readiness is supported by improvements implemented over several years as part of its broader water security and service reliability program. These include developing alternative and supplemental water sources, increasing treatment and storage capacity, rehabilitating pipelines, reducing water losses, and improving pressure management and network operations. The company also maintains contingency measures that can be used when operating conditions require them. These initiatives were not undertaken solely in response to a particular El Niño episode; they help strengthen the system against a range of supply and climate-related challenges.

4. How is Maynilad better prepared than during previous El Niño episodes?

Compared with 2019, Maynilad now has additional treatment and storage capacity, expanded supplemental water sources, lower water losses, and improved distribution network management. These improvements have strengthened its ability to maintain stable water service even under reduced raw water allocations. They provide greater flexibility in using and distributing available supply and help reduce the risk and potential extent of service disruptions, although they cannot eliminate every risk from prolonged dry conditions or other operating constraints.

5. Where does Maynilad get its water, aside from Angat Dam?

Angat Dam remains Maynilad’s principal raw water source. The company has also developed supplemental and alternative sources, including water from Laguna Lake treated at its Putatan and Poblacion facilities and potable reused water produced through its NEW WATER program. Other available augmentation and contingency sources may be used as operating conditions require. The contribution of each source depends on its operating status, production capability, raw water conditions, and the areas it can serve.

6. Why is reducing water losses important?

Water that is lost through leaks and other causes cannot be fully used by customers. By finding and repairing leaks, replacing aging pipelines, improving network management, and addressing illegal connections, Maynilad can recover water that would otherwise be lost. This helps make more effective use of available supply and strengthens service reliability without depending only on new raw water sources.

7. What role do reservoirs and better network operations play?

Reservoirs provide storage that helps Maynilad manage variations in production and customer demand. Meanwhile, pressure management and network optimization allow the company to distribute water more efficiently across its service area. Alongside reliable treatment operations, these measures give Maynilad more flexibility when supply conditions change.

8. Why should customers use water responsibly if service is stable?

Responsible water use matters at all times, not only during El Niño. Avoiding unnecessary wastage helps make the most of available water resources, particularly when rainfall is reduced. Simple steps include turning off taps when not in use, promptly fixing household leaks, using only the water needed for everyday tasks, and reporting leaks in public areas. Customers should continue using the water they need for drinking, hygiene, sanitation, and other essential activities.

9. Where can customers get updates or report water-related concerns?

Customers can check Maynilad’s official website and verified social media channels for the latest service announcements and customer advisories. To report leaks, suspected illegal connections, or service concerns, they may contact Maynilad through Hotline 1626 or its official customer assistance channels. For any scheduled service interruption, customers should refer to the applicable area-specific advisory rather than assume that general information about El Niño applies to their location.

item.title: Maynilad sustains El Niño readiness after system withstands July Angat low
item.dc:creator: Danica Pagarigan
item.description: West Zone concessionaire Maynilad Water Services, Inc. (Maynilad) continues to strengthen its El Niño preparedness even as Angat Dam has recovered from its July lows, citing reduced water losses as the primary contributor to lowering its operational reliance on Angat, complemented by source diversification, stronger treatment capability, and greater network flexibility. Angat Dam fell to […]
item.content:encoded:
West Zone concessionaire Maynilad Water Services, Inc. (Maynilad) continues to strengthen its El Niño preparedness even as Angat Dam has recovered from its July lows, citing reduced water losses as the primary contributor to lowering its operational reliance on Angat, complemented by source diversification, stronger treatment capability, and greater network flexibility.

Angat Dam fell to 150.42 meters in July 2026—lower than the 157.96-meter level recorded during the 2019 water crisis, when rotational water supply was implemented. This year, however, Maynilad was able to manage the lower dam level without resorting to rotational interruptions.

Angat has since recovered to above 207 meters following rains during the wet season, but Maynilad said continued preparedness remains necessary as El Niño conditions may bring below-normal rainfall and tighter raw water conditions in the coming months.

“The experience earlier this year showed why we have been investing in a more resilient water supply system,” said Maynilad Chief Operating Officer Christopher Jaime T. Lichauco. “When Angat dropped below its 2019 level, we had more tools available to manage the situation—from lower water losses and alternative sources to stronger treatment capability and greater network flexibility. We are continuing these measures as El Niño conditions persist and we prepare for potentially drier months ahead.”

The biggest contributor to reducing Maynilad’s operational reliance on Angat has been its intensified Non-Revenue Water (NRW) reduction program, which allows more of the water already available in the system to reach customers and reduces the need for additional raw water supply. As of June 2026, the company had reduced daily water losses by more than 150 million liters per day compared with June 2025, making more water available for distribution to customers.

Maynilad has also progressively diversified its water sources through Laguna Lake, deep wells, modular treatment plants, and NEW WATER facilities. Based on treatment capacity, Angat now accounts for about 83% of Maynilad’s supply capacity, compared with 100% historically.

The company has likewise strengthened its South system, particularly its Laguna Lake-based facilities, through treatment and process improvements designed to make alternative supply more reliable under changing raw water quality conditions. These investments provide added flexibility in managing available supply across the network when Angat becomes constrained.

Maynilad said it will continue to monitor source conditions, optimize available supply, and coordinate with government agencies on water allocation and supply management as El Niño conditions persist.

“Improved dam levels give us more buffer, but we continue to prepare because El Niño can still affect rainfall and raw water availability in the coming months,” Lichauco said. “Our objective is to keep strengthening the system so we can manage changing conditions while protecting service reliability for our customers.” Maynilad also encouraged customers to continue using water responsibly and to report visible leaks or illegal connections.

PHOTO CAPTION: Maynilad’s Poblacion Water Treatment Plant in Muntinlupa City draws raw water from Laguna Lake and forms part of the company’s strengthened South system, helping diversify water sources and reduce operational reliance on Angat Dam amid El Niño.

item.content:encoded:
West Zone concessionaire Maynilad Water Services, Inc. (Maynilad) is offering septic tank cleaning services to its residential and semi-business customers this October in select parts of Caloocan, Las Piñas, Manila, Muntinlupa, Parañaque, Pasay, Quezon City, Valenzuela, and Cavite Province at no extra cost.

Maynilad’s sanitation program is one of the company’s efforts to lessen pollution loading into Metro Manila’s river systems. “We ask our customers to avail of this service, as it will help to protect community health and the environment,” said Engr. Zmel Grabillo, Maynilad’s Head of Wastewater Management.

Customers residing in Barangay 80, 89, 138, 139,142 to 146, 148, 149, 151, 160, and 162 in Caloocan; Brgy. Almanza I, Manuyo II, Pamplona 1, Pamplona III, Pillar Village, Pulang Lupa I, Pulang Lupa II, Talon I, and Talon II in Las Piñas; Brgy. Port Area, Quiapo, San Miguel, San Nicolas, Sta. Cruz, and Sta. Mesa in Manila; Brgy. Don Carlos, Maricaban, Pildera 1, San Rafael, and San Roque in Pasay; Brgy. Cupang in Muntinlupa; Brgy. Don Galo, San Martin de Porres, Sun Valley, and Tambo in Parañaque; Brgy. Commonwealth, Nagkaisang Nayon, Paltok, Payatas, Salvacion, San Antonio, San Bartolome, San Isidro, Sta. Lucia, Sta. Monica, and Sto. Niño in Quezon City; and Brgy. Dalandanan, Isla, Mabolo, Malinta, Maysan, Parada, Pasolo, Poblacion, Polo, Rincon, and Tagalag in Valenzuela may avail of Maynilad’s desludging service.

Moreover, some Maynilad customers in Cavite Province, particularly Brgy. Aniban II, Habay I, Kaingin, Ligas II, Ligas III, Mabolo II, Mabolo III, Maliksi II, Maliksi III, Mambog II to Mambog IV, Malino III, Real I, Real II, Salinas I, San Nicolas III, and Sineguelasan in Bacoor City; Brgy. Anabu I-C, Bayan Luma II, Malagasanag II-A, Malagasang II-B, Malagasang II-D, Malagasang II-F, Tanzang Luma I to Tanzang Luma VI, Toclong I-A, and Toclong I-B in Imus City may avail of the company’s septic tank cleaning services at no extra cost. Septic tank cleaning service normally costs around Php 4,700 per truck.

Maynilad customers interested in availing of the company’s septic tank cleaning service may call the Maynilad Hotline 1626 to determine the requirements and procedures. Additional information is also available in the company’s website, www.mayniladwater.com.ph, and social media accounts (X: @maynilad, Facebook: /MayniladWater).

Maynilad operates the largest water concession by population served within a single concession area in the Philippines. It is a concessionaire of the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS) for the West Zone of the Greater Manila Area, which is composed of the cities of Manila (certain portions), Quezon City (certain portions), Makati (west of South Super Highway), Caloocan, Pasay, Parañaque, Las Piñas, Muntinlupa, Valenzuela, Navotas and Malabon, all in Metro Manila; the cities of Cavite, Bacoor and Imus, and the municipalities of Kawit, Noveleta and Rosario, all in Cavite Province.

item.title: Maynilad cuts daily water losses by more than 150 MLD year-on-year
item.dc:creator: Danica Pagarigan
item.description: West Zone concessionaire Maynilad Water Services, Inc. (Maynilad) reduced its daily volume of non-revenue water (NRW) by more than 150 million liters per day (MLD) as of June 2026 compared with June 2025, making more water available for distribution to customers. The recovered volume is equivalent to the output of a water treatment plant and […]
item.content:encoded:
West Zone concessionaire Maynilad Water Services, Inc. (Maynilad) reduced its daily volume of non-revenue water (NRW) by more than 150 million liters per day (MLD) as of June 2026 compared with June 2025, making more water available for distribution to customers.

The recovered volume is equivalent to the output of a water treatment plant and can meet the daily water requirements of around 770,000 people.

The improvement was achieved through targeted leak repairs and rehabilitation of tertiary, secondary, and primary pipelines, with water loss reductions recorded across several areas within Maynilad’s concession.

“Reducing water losses enables us to make better use of the water already available in our system. This becomes even more important as we prepare for possible supply constraints associated with El Niño, since every liter we recover helps strengthen our supply buffer without requiring an equivalent increase in water production,” said Maynilad Chief Operating Officer Christopher Jaime T. Lichauco.

Maynilad’s average NRW level likewise improved to 31.5% in the first half of 2026, from 36.7% in the same period last year, reflecting continued progress in reducing physical and commercial water losses across its distribution network.

For 2026, Maynilad allotted ₱7.7 billion for its NRW management program, covering pipe and meter replacement, active leakage control, district metered area establishment and maintenance, and network diagnostic activities. The company is targeting an NRW level of 25% by 2027 as part of its MWSS-approved Business Plan. Based on its current performance trajectory, Maynilad is on track to end 2026 with an NRW level of about 25%, supporting its goal of achieving a 29% average NRW for the full year.

PHOTO CAPTION: Maynilad personnel inspect ongoing pipeline rehabilitation works as part of the company’s leak repair and network upgrade activities. These interventions helped reduce Maynilad’s non-revenue water (NRW) volume by more than 150 million liters per day (MLD) as of June 2026 compared with June 2025, making more water available for distribution. The recovered volume can meet the daily water requirements of around 770,000 people.
